h: Below decks and beyond the quay
p: Trincomalee has had a remarkable life since she left Bombay. Built from teak at a time when British oak was running short, she spent decades as a training ship for young sailors and even carried a different name, Foudroyant, for much of the 20th century before her original name was restored. She arrived in Hartlepool in the late 1980s for a long and painstaking restoration, and the care that went into it shows in every beam and rope.

Once you're aboard, take it slowly. Headroom drops sharply on the lower decks, so taller visitors will be ducking more than once, and the ladders between decks are steep in proper sailing-ship fashion. Have a look at the cannon on the gun deck, then picture the noise and smoke of a broadside fired in that cramped space. It's a real lightbulb moment for kids who've only seen tall ships in films.

How long should you allow? Most families will happily fill half a day between the ship, the quayside streets and the Museum of Hartlepool, and longer if the children take to the playship. It's a good one for grandparents and grandkids together, with plenty for history buffs and plenty to climb on for the little ones.

If you've still got energy afterwards, the Headland is a short drive away, with St Hilda's Church, the old town walls and big views out over the North Sea. Seaton Carew's long sandy beach is just down the coast too, handy for a blow-out walk and a bag of chips to finish the day.
